speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The matter of urgent and pressing necessity arises from the cabinet's overturning of the Anti-Inflation Board's decision on the postal workers contract and in particular the board's complete distortion of the purpose of "historical relationship" as found on page 23 of the white paper on inflation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to introduce a motion dealing with an important issue.
Since social stability in Canada is deeply undermined by some anti-inflation government measures rejected by the workers who have no confidence in the government statements on price controls, and since it is urgent not only to control but to reduce prices to enable consumers to buy available products, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That this House consider as soon as possible the opportunity of applying a compensated discount to consumer prices, which discount would cover all essential products and would be based on the difference between purchasing power and production value, thereby ending inflation.

The House resumed, from Thursday, December 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-41, respecting the stabilization of net proceeds from the production and sale of western grain and to amend certain statutes in consequence thereof, be read the third time and do pass.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at adjournment last night I was attempting to analyse the minister's statement of December 4, 1974, in terms of what he said about the four objectives of Bill C-41. I want to deal now with objective No. 3 which he cited in that statement, namely, that Bill C-41 would be complementary to the development of the livestock industry. It is difficult for me to understand what, if anything, it will do for the development of the livestock industry.
Grain Stabilization
We can all generally agree that recurring booms and busts in grain markets have a disruptive influence on the livestock industry. Because the grains stabilization plan purposely avoids interfering with the market forces which the minister mentioned in his statement, the plan will do nothing to protect the livestock industry from those disruptive influences. Stabilization payments made at a time when grain prices tumble and markets are glutted will not change the fact that the low-priced grain is there to be diverted into the feeding of additional livestock. When basic market forces dictate that grain prices are high because of scarcity, the livestock producers suffer. We have seen this cycle repeated time after time to the detriment of both the grain and the livestock industries. I therefore submit it is wrong to say that a plan which leaves the basic market forces intact will contribute to the development of the livestock industry.
The fourth and final objective the minister listed in his statement of December 4 was that the grain stabilization plan would be based on a set of principles consistent with general objectives for agriculture which could be applied to other commodity groups. Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, that has to be the most incomprehensible statement ever made on the proposed grain stabilization plan. I challenge any hon. member to find any other example among the long list of private or public insurance or social security programs in this country which is based on a set of principles similar to that proposed in the grain stabilization plan.
In fact, Bill C-41 has its priorities backwards. The authors of the plan have adopted as principles what are considered to be beneficial side-effects of other programs to protect individuals or groups against uncertainties and vagaries inherent in our economic and social system. It is well known that programs designed to protect individuals and groups against financial losses resulting from accident, illness, unemployment, old age, and so on, have the beneficial side-effect of preventing a sharp decline in spending. Because such programs tend to prevent the economy going into a tailspin in that they maintain aggregate spending, economists have dubbed them "built-in stabilizers". The primary purpose of the program is the protection of individuals. The factor of economic stabilization is a side-effect. The proposed grain stabilization plan, however, has as its primary purpose the aggregate stabilization of the cash flow from grain sales. Protection of individual farmers would be a side-effect of the plan and is by no means assured. This is why we submit that Bill C-41 has its priorities backwards.
It is ironic that the statement should be made that Bill C-41 is based on a set of principles consistent with the general objectives of agriculture which could be applied to other commodity groups. If this were so, why did the government see fit to put through the two-price wheat act and introduce Bill C-50, an act to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act? If the principles on which Bill C-41 are based are so sound, why not apply them to cattle, hogs and sheep, industrial milk, industrial cream, corn and soy beans? Those commodities are not governed on the basis of the principles the minister has embodied in this bill.

December 12, 1975
Grain Stabilization
I think it should be made abundantly clear that the government of Manitoba does not support the principles upon which the proposed grain stabilization plan are based. The government of Saskatchewan does not support them. Neither do members of the official opposition or members of my party. Farmers, by the thousands, do not support them. The farm organizations which the minister feels are supporting his legislation are, in fact, so fed up with waiting to get some meaningful stabilization legislation that they are throwing their hands up and saying, "Well, it is better than nothing." How the minister can consider this as amounting to wholehearted support for Bill C-41 is beyond me.
We cannot support the principle that the maintenance of an aggregate cash flow is an important public objective while the provision of basic security to individual producers is merely incidental. We have endeavoured to persuade the government to adopt a number of amendments, but the government has refused to accept any but a couple of minor ones. Even if the amendments we proposed had been accepted, the legislation would have remained deficient. Surely the provision of basic security to the individual producer must come first. Everything else is incidental.
Let me illustrate the degree to which the legislation is unfair in other areas. The minister did come around to our point of view, expressed four years ago, that any income stabilization program should be based on net income, not on gross income. He has come at least part of the way by basing pay-outs on the net cash flow. This means that the farmers real and legitimate costs of production have to be taken into account in order to arrive at their net income. Although we tried in committee and during the report stage to persuade the government that it is excluding legitimate costs of production in the most arbitrary and unfair manner, in terms of arriving at the point at which a pay-out had to be made from the fund, our efforts were unsuccessful.
Mr. Speaker, in every kind of business, under present accounting practice items such as depreciation on farm buildings, farm machinery and equipment are considered to form part of the cost of production. But this is not recognized in the bill before us. If Your Honour has had any dealings with grain producers you will know that depreciation of farm machinery and equipment is a major item each year. Even more unfairly, the bill in no way specifies that interest charges on buildings, machinery and equipment may be considered a legitimate expense in computing a farmer's net income from grain sales.
The parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), tried to persuade me in the House during the report stage that the legislation could be construed as meaning that interest charges would be covered. I still cannot find support for his contention after reading the bill. I believe the hon. member is wrong and if die legislation passes, interest payments by farmers on buildings, machinery and equipment will not be allowed as a cost of production.
I now turn to the 2 per cent levy which farmers will have to pay. Everyone I have talked to has concluded that this levy is a premium which has to be paid in order to secure coverage under the plan. But the minister says this levy
(Mr. Benjamin.]
cannot be counted as a cost of production. The premiums a farmer pays for the insurance of his property, crop insurance, and so on, are allowed as legitimate deductions for income tax purposes. They are included in the cost of production. This is a practice accepted under all normal accounting procedures, it is followed by farm management clubs, and so on, but not under the proposed grain stabilization act. The cost of this premium can amount to $500 a year and it is, of course, a cash expense. The minister talks about cash flow. If the payment of interest on farm buildings and machinery is not a cash flow out, I do not know what is. The 2 per cent deduction for the levy is a cash expense that affects the grain producer's cash flow, but it is not covered by Bill C-41.
Let me talk for a moment or two about how this legislation is going to be unfair to producers because it covers all grain producers, not grain producers as individuals. There is an instance occurring right now along a branch line in my constituency where the CPR has not run a train for two weeks and says it is not going to run one for several more weeks. I had telephone calls from three producers along that line last night-one of them lives half a mile from his elevator and has a malting barley permit-and these producers have a total of four carloads anc( have to deliver to the next branch line, an additional haul of 30 to 40 miles for each of them. The additional hauling costs will use up the premium on the malting barley.
Those producers are unable to deliver their grain to the delivery point because the CPR says they are not going to run any more trains over that track for a few weeks. I hope the minister is making a note of this because I will phone his office about it later today. On this particular branch line somewhere in the order of 10 of 20 carloads of malting barley will have to be delivered to another branch line, meaning an additional haul of 20 to 50 miles for each producer. If the grain stabilization plan were in effect and those farmers were unable to make their deliveries, their effect and those farmers were unable to make their deliveries, their income would drop. Their cash flow would drop, to use the minister's term. But they will not be protected under this program unless every grain producer's cash income drops.
The province of Manitoba, in its submissions to the committee, and also the submissions of the Manitoba crop insurance board to the Senate committee, made not only what I consider most practical and proper proposals for a grain incomes stabilization plan but also offered to administer the plan for the government with only a small increase in the staff of the crop insurance board already in place. They offered to administer it on an individual basis so that farmers could pay their premiums and would know what coverage they were buying. They would be protected against losses due to economic circumstances over which they have no control.
In other words, our grain income stabilization program would be integrated and meshed with crop insurance so that the farmer would have complete protection against natural hazards under crop insurance and against the hazards of the marketplace and prices, whether they be domestic or international. The farmer would have individual coverage, and that is the only way this kind of
December 12, 1975

legislation would be fair and proper. I agree with the position taken by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and other members of the official opposition. We have taken the same position, that the program should be on an individual basis. It can be on an individual basis, and why the minister insists on an aggregate basis is beyond me. It betrays the whole principle of income insurance, income protection, income stabilization or whatever you want to call it.
Take the case of producers of grain, rapeseed, and so on, in northern Saskatchewan. They could have a good yield, which would mean they had no coverage under crop insurance. But the yield could be of poor quality, consisting of low protein wheat or barley not fit for malting, for which there is no market. On the other hand, grain producers in the rest of the region might have a good yield of high quality grain and they can make large deliveries. The Canadian Wheat Board and purchasers of non-board grains will buy the higher quality crops. I am sure the honourable member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Cadieu) can verify that the income of farmers in that area would drop because they make low deliveries due to economic circumstances over which they have no control, and under this legislation they will not be protected.
The only way these producers would get a pay-out is if the total net income of the entire Wheat Board region falls below the previous five-year average. Under this legislation you could have 5,000, 10,000 or 15,000 grain producers whose income drops through no fault of their own. If this drop in income is not due to natural hazards, they are not covered. Surely that is the wrong kind of stabilization program to have.
This bill needs to go back to committee and the minister should agree to make fundamental changes in the legislation. Once the legislation is in place, Mr. Speaker, we all know that no matter how unfair it is and how badly it is working, it will take years to get such fundamental changes as this made. The province of Saskatchewan has expressed support for the position taken by the province of Manitoba, and I am confident that the province of Alberta will do likewise.
This program should be integrated with the crop insurance program and farmers should be protected on an individual basis. Then they will know what they are buying, what protection they will get and against what hazards they are covered. They will not have to wait until the entire region suffers before getting protection. The minister can hand over administration of this program to the crop insurance boards of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and also British Columbia because the Peace River district is in the designated area.
I and my colleagues are unable to support this legislation in its present form, and I regret that very much. The minister has made some changes from the legislation of 1971. He did learn his lesson a little then, but he still retreats from the kind of income stabilization program that is needed. He still refuses to depart from the nineteenth century concepts about the free play of the open market, and so on, and protecting the grain producer or any other producer from the hazards and fluctuations of so-called basic market forces. I do not want to be party to legislation that is designed to reinforce systems that continually get
Grain Stabilization
grain producers or livestock producers into difficulties with boom and bust cycles. The grain stabilization program of the minister will not level out and protect the incomes of individual grain producers in times of boom and bust. Indeed, the legislation is deliberately designed not to do so.
I see my time is almost up, so I would urge the minister to reconsider the legislation. Let him take it back to the drawing board and re-examine the submissions of the government of Manitoba, supported by many other submissions and by the province of Saskatchewan. I am confident that Alberta would also support it if the minister discussed it with them. Let him redraft the legislation and implement a grain stabilization program that covers farmers on an individual basis and is administered in conjunction with crop insurance. It would then be welcomed by members on all sides of the House, by individual producers and by all farm organizations.
If the minister fails to do this, he should not be surprised if there is lack of urgency on my part and on the part of many other members of the House to deal with this legislation. In fact, if the legislation does not see the light of day it will not hurt my feelings, and my impression is that it will not hurt the feelings of the grain producers in western Canada. Indeed, they are yawning over it. They are bored by it. They cannot understand it. It is too complicated for the minister to explain, and it is certainly beyond me. If you read some of the provisions of the bill you will end up talking to yourself. To accept that and to try to explain it to grain producers in order that they will be interested in taking part in the program is an exercise in frustration.
The history of the grain stabilization program has been well noted for this House. For years the grain producers, provincial governments and farm organizations have been asking for income protection in relation to prices and markets, as well as in relation to natural hazards. One would think the minister would finally realize that this is the kind of stabilization program these people want, rather than the proposal contained in this legislation.
I hope other members of the House will take part in this debate in order to bring these things to the minister's attention in a last-ditch effort to persuade him that the legislation should not pass in this form but, rather, should be sent back to the standing committee to be redrafted in line with the proposal made by the province of Manitoba. The minister would find that such a proposal would be acceptable to the members of the three opposition parties and to the provincial governments and, most important, acceptable to the individual grain producers in western Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
That is right. It seems to me the minister has been too busy with some of his other portfolios to take a real interest in piloting this bill through the House.
I go along with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) when he said yesterday that agriculture should be under the purview of one minister rather than being the subject of divided responsibility, as is the case today. Only if we have one minister in charge of agriculture can we have the co-ordination and co-operation necessary to make agriculture really go in this country.
First of all, we should consider what this bill does Let me make it clear at the outset that it does not provide stability of income to the individual producer. What it does is attempt to stabilize the over-all economy of western Canada and make a relatively table tax base for the government. This is not what the producer in western Canada is interested in or wants.
When the bill was tabled for first reading, I obtained a number of copies and mailed them to various farm organizations in my constituency, as well as to the reeves and secretary-treasurers of the municipalities, and asked them to let me have their comments. I received one reply asking for further information. I made some inquiries later during the summer of those individuals and organizations in an attempt to find out why I had not heard from them. Their answers were very simple. The bill was such a complex and complicated piece of legislation that they could not understand it; therefore, they were not in a position to ask questions or to make comments. How can one comment on a bill that cannot be understood?
In June of this year the Standing Committee on Agriculture travelled to western Canada and visited the major cities in the three prairie provinces. Prior to that visit we requested farm organizations and individuals to make presentations. Some 18 organizations and representatives from the departments of agriculture for the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan made presentations. Without exception, their first comment was about the complexity of the legislation. All these organizations and representatives of wheat pools and the National Farmers' Union said they really could not discuss the bill with their grass-roots members because of its complexity. This was after representatives of the Department of Agriculture had travelled throughout the west making presentations as to how the bill would work and how it would affect the prairie farmer. A similar presentation was made to our committee, during the course of its hearings, which included a series of charts and figures. Those charts and figures did not explain the bill.
Time will not permit me to mention all the points that concerned the groups which made representations to the committee. Other speakers have already touched upon some of them, but I should like to mention one or two. The first matter involves the question of including depreciation as an expense. The minister and his parliamentary secretary attempted to give an explanation of why depreciation (Mr. Neil.)
should not be included. Farmers in western Canada will tell you that depreciation of their equipment and buildings is a major expense of carrying on farming operations. Briefs also touched on the suggestion that interest should be included as an expense of carrying on operations. They did not ask that interest on land be included as an expense but, rather, the interest on their capital investment for machinery and on their borrowings from the banks for their day to day operations. The minister has not seen fit to include these items as expenses.
The minister has spoken of voluntary compliance with the plan. As the plan stands, farmers are included unless they opt out. They can opt out and in only once, and then they are in for all time. This is something that concerns producers in the prairie region. They like a voluntary plan, and do not like to be forced to participate in something they do not like and do not understand. The majority of those who made presentations were concerned about the global aspect of the plan, as well as the fact that pay-outs under the plan are only triggered when the average cash flow in the entire Canadian Wheat Pool area is less than the previous five-year average. The majority of the representatives of these organizations spoke of a regional basis on which to trigger the payments. Almost without exception, when questioned each organization and each individual indicated that an ideal plan is one based on individual participation.
I should like to refer to the minutes of the meetings held, one in Saskatoon and one in Winnipeg. I shall refer to issue No. 53 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, dated Friday, June 20, 1975. This is a presentation by the Manitoba Farm Bureau. It reads in part:
In discussions with grain producers it often becomes evident that there is some tendency to reject the idea of participation in the plan because as it stands it does not provide for application of it on a regional basis.
A little later in the same issue, at page 81, in a presentation made by Mr. Otto Fielman who is a grain producer from the area of Rosenfeld, Manitoba, and also a director of the Manitoba Wheat Pool, we find this statement:
Farmers are independent business operators that want a stabilization plan to fill their individual needs, and not a lottery type chance of payment which has no connection with their own operation.
In issue No. 52 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence, at page 42 Mr. Lemon, a representative of the National Farmers' Union, local 611, had this to say:
To average the entire Wheat Board area appears to be ridiculous as a protection for individuals or localized areas.
Mr. Speaker, the bill covers six different grains-wheat, oats, barley, rye, flax and rapeseed. As I mentioned before, payment is triggered when the net cash flow in the entire Canadian Wheat Board area in a particular year is less than the previous five-year average. But consider the situation of the various producers in the prairies. There are many who specialize in producing a particular type of grain, depending on the area in which their farm is located.
December 12, 1975

There are areas where people specialize in the growing of rapeseed or feed grains or flax. Let us suppose a farmer specializes in one of these particular crops and in one year or, perhaps in two or three years, the volume of sales is low and the price of the particular grain is low, yet the price of the other five grains remains high and the volume of sales is high. Under those circumstances, the average net cash flow in the entire Wheat Board area would exceed the five-year average and there would be no payment out. In other words, there would be producers who, because they specialized in producing a particular type of grain, would not be able to receive benefits under the plan.
If it worked on a regional basis, there would still be problems similar to those if we used the entire Canadian Wheat Board area. Many members here, and most producers, will recall PFAA legislation, which I understand started on a global basis and then worked down to a regional basis. With the PFAA program on a regional basis there were many situations in which particular farmers who were just across the border from the area where a PFAA payment was being made did not receive a cent. A farmer across the road may have a much better crops than them, but because they were in a particular region they were not able to receive payments.
What I am saying is that the utilization of a regional basis is not a fair way to operate a plan. Our party and most producers in western Canada feel that an individual plan is the only basis on which we should be stabilizing income. The minister, of course, would not accept this concept. He suggested that we should put the bill through as it is and then we could make changes. But why put through a bad bill? Why put through a bill that is not acceptable to the producers, the people who will be participating in the program? The producers in western Canada do not want a bill they do not understand. It seems to me the function of any committee is to consider legislation, to listen to representations by interested people and to take heed of what they say. We heard many representations. I think we, as members of the committee, heeded the representations but the minister did not.
This bill is drafted in such a manner that it is impossible to amend it. The minister should have withdrawn the bill and submitted a new one. He cannot use the excuse that time was important because, as I said at the outset, this bill has been before the House off and on, for over a year. So there has been plenty of time for him to consider withdrawing the bill and bringing in a new one. I am sure that if he had done so, the bill would have been passed quite a long time ago.
It is intersting to examine the figures that were presented to members of the committee by representatives of the Department of Agriculture. I am referring to a historical review which covers the period 1954 to 1974 based on actual production and the assumption that this plan was in existence during that time. During that 20-year period, producers in the Canadian Wheat Board area, had this plan been in existence, would have contributed in the order of $441.6 million.
However, if we look further at the chart we find it would have been necessary for the government to lend money to the fund from time to time. It would have been lent at varying rates. In the period 1954 to 1959 the rate would
Grain Stabilization
have been 4 per cent; in the period 1960 to 1969 the rate would have been 5 per cent; and in the period 1970 to 1974 the rate would have been 7 per cent. What do we find? We find that during the same period the producers would have been called upon to pay interest of $210.1 million to the government. In other words, their contribution to the fund would have been $441.6 million and they would have had to pay interest of $210.1 million.
Almost half of the producers' levy would have been used to pay interest to the government, leaving only $221.5 million of the producers' money to be used for stabilization. Granted, the contributions of the producers drew interest which totalled $7.4 million. The average amount that would have been paid into the plan annually by the government during that period was $43.5 million. During this period, of course, the plan was not in operation, but under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, under PFAA and under some other schemes, the government has contributed some $70 million annually. These schemes have all been phased out or cancelled. On a historical average, using the stabilization bill, the government would be contributing some $43.5 million annually.
As I stated earlier, this program should be administered on an individual basis. There are several ways in which this could be accomplished . I will mention only two. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) will be presenting a third plan later this afternoon. The first alternative I am suggesting is based upon a 2 per cent contribution by the producer and a 4 per cent contribution by the government, but the producers' and the government's contributions would be put into the individual account of the producer and to that account would be added the accrued interest as it built up. We are suggesting, as well, that gross sales would be up to $35,000. If you use that basis, at the end of the first year the producers' levy would be $700 and the government's levy would be $1,400. At the end of the first year the producer would have in his account $2,100 plus interest. At the end of the second year the producer would have in his account, assuming there were no withdrawals, up to $1,400 and the government's levy would be $2,800, for a total of up to $4,200, plus interest.
The operation of the plan would be based on income insurance. The producer would receive a payment from the plan under the following circumstances. At the beginning of the crop year, when the Canadian Wheat Board establishes its initial price, the Department of Agriculture would fix a maximum insurable price for the six different grains based on the five-year average price and the cost of production. The producer, based on the contributions in his account, could insure for the amount per bushel up to a maximum being the difference between the initial price announced by the Canadian Wheat Board and the maximum insurable price fixed by the Department of Agriculture. The producer would then be entitled to receive payment of an amount per bushel equal to the difference between the maximum insurable price and the final realized CWB price per bushel or the amount for which he insured.
Let me give an example. Using crop insurance statistics, if the average yield in the crop district for wheat is, say, 25 bushels per acre, and if the initial price fixed by CWB in

December 12, 1975
Grain Stabilization
the spring is $2.25 a bushel, if the Department of Agriculture fixes the maximum insurable price at $3 a bushel the producer could insure for the amount per bushel up to a maximum difference between the maximum insurable price and the initial price; in other words, $3 minus $2.25, or 75 cents a bushel. In his first year of coverage, the producer would have a maximum coverage on 2,800 bushels, or 107 acres at 26 bushels an acre. If the final realized CWB price were $2.50 a bushel, the producer would receive 2,800 bushels at 50 cents, or $1,400.
According to the second alternative, a separate account would be set up as before, but rather than using Statistics Canada officials to wander from farm to farm picking up statistics, certain colour coded income tax returns could be used and the Department of National Revenue could inject these figures from the returns into a computer and get an accurate figure on the aggregate net income and the expenses. Payment under this program would be triggered, first of all, when the aggregate net income or the net cash flow in the entire CWB area was less than the five-year average, or if the net income of the individual for the particular year was less than his five-year average. The producer would have the right to elect whether to apply for a payment under the program and he could do so when he filled his income tax return each year. On his retirement, whatever remained in his account, plus interest, would be returned to him, less the benefits he had received.
Neither system would involve government loans. Such a program would be actuarially sound, it would save millions of dollars in interest, and I am sure it would be acceptable. These are only two of a number of possible individual programs. They would be understandable to the producer. I plead with the minister in charge of the Wheat Board to give serious consideration to accepting one or other of these plans in substitution of the plan which is before us. I suggest that he withdraw the bill and bring in another one some time in the near future which would be more acceptable.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us attempts to stabilize the net proceeds of grain farmers in western Canada. I disagree with the fundamental principle of the bill, which is an aggregate pay-out as opposed to individual compensation. It seems to me that Bill C-41 is just a means which the government is using to try to replace some of the legislation which has been taken off the statute books. As the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) said, the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and deficiency payments amounted to about $70 million per year.
(Mr. Neil.)
Federal assistance is certainly warranted, in view of the importance of the western grain industry to Canada and to the world. I suggest that we need a list of priorities for the western grain industry, but surely Bill C-41 is a long way down the list. As we travelled across the prairies last summer, it was said many times that no one really understands this bill. That is because of its language. With regard to persons deemed not to be actual producers, clause 5(8) of the bill reads as follows:
Where an actual producer who is not eligible to participate under this act makes an application for a permit book together with an eligible actual producer, the actual producer who is not eligible shall, for the purposes of this act, be deemed to be a producer who is not an actual producer.
Is it any wonder farmers threw up their hands when they were asked to comment on this very complicated bill? The minister has compared this bill with fire insurance. The only difference is that if a house burns down, its owner is paid for it; but under this bill, if a farmer loses a crop he will not necessarily receive any money. We have had many years' experience with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and over the years the act was brought closer and closer to an individual basis. With the experience the government has had of administering that act, I suggest it could well bring this grain stabilization bill toward an individual basis such as we have with crop insurance. It works very successfully in western Canada.
It is hard to overemphasize the importance of western grain to this country. I am looking at the daily Thunder Bay outward traffic report for December 6, 1975. There were 1,170 cars. For the same day, in Vancouver there were 511. There are about 1,700 cars of grain per day being unloaded. Of course, this year everything is moving well. It will not be a record year, but exports will probably be 600 million bushels with another 200 million moving within the country by rail for domestic purposes.
Recent world trends in grain stocks underscore the extent of Canada's food power. Supplies in the world are steadily declining, and for the first time the United States has established a national grain export policy in place of the free rein which was allowed commercial grain exporters in the past. We see the Americans, who are our main competitors in grain exports, negotiating long-term agreements with our good customers, Russia, Japan and Poland. These deals indicate how eager foreign countries are to nail down the world's grain supplies. They are buying fixed volumes in an orderly fashion.
I suggest the Canadian government could do much more for this country along that line. Canada and the United States now account for 70 per cent of the world export of grains. I indicated how much grain was moving for export right now; some 1,700 cars a day are being unloaded. This is going to mean something over $3 billion in exports for Canada. This is over 10 per cent of our total exports. When you consider the multiplier effect of grain sales in this country, one can see that the federal government could well afford to put more money back into the industry. In a world of growing scarcity, Canadians must be made aware of the great power of their grain industry. When ministers of this government go abroad with a little wheat in their pockets, doors are opened to them. Wheat, more than anything else we possess, will open doors for our ministers. The United States ability to produce food has regained for
December 12, 1975

that country much of the diplomatic clout it lost over the Viet Nam war.
Our country is going the stabilization-supply management route. This scheme, like other stabilization schemes, must inevitably lead to border restrictions. As the United States scales down its so-called give-away programs under public law 480, new opportunities will open for Canada. New cash customers will look to Canada for the kind of grain we grow. Saskatchewan is by far the largest grain producer in Canada. I shall, therefore, put on record part of the telex communication Mr. Kaeding, the minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan, sent to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. He said:
The Saskatchewan government believes that the whole philosophy behind Bill C-41 is subject to serious question since it does not relate payments under the program to need but rather to historical price levels ...
The plan does not provide individual, commodity or regional stability. It neglects the geographic and climatic factors which influence the production of various grains throughout the prairies. The implicit assumption is that the prairies are a homogeneous area. This assumption is not valid . ..
If present levels of support for livestock production remain in effect once Bill C-41 is passed, the excessive shifting of resources between livestock and grain production will continue.
He then said:
Interest depreciation and labour cost must be included in any reasonable computation of costs for producers.
This matter was mentioned in the agriculture committee hearings. The communication went on to say:
The use of the Income Tax Department as an administration mechanism should be examined since it could be more efficient and reduce administration costs-
Right now, western resources and resourceful westerners are keeping this country afloat. As I said before, grain export sales this year will amount to over $3.5 billion, or 10 per cent of Canada's exports. If anything interrupts or shuts down the flow of this commodity, the Canadian dollar would be devalued overnight. The word I hear from agricultural producers in my constituency is, "Please do not help us any more with government stabilization plans because they do not seem to have served any useful purpose in western Canada." Actually, since the government introduced its so-called stabilization plan we have seen more violent fluctuations in cattle prices than ever before.
Very simply, grain producers need some means, in years of high income, of deferring tax-free money to an individual, registered stabilization fund. This money could be withdrawn in years of low income. Grain producers already are given the privilege of deferring grain sales from one year to the next. I suggest that this program could well be expanded and money paid to farmers on their deferred grain sales should earn interest. There is a need, in the agricultural industry of Canada from coast to coast, for a type of vehicle through which individuals or corporations whose primary business is that of agriculture can be encouraged to save funds, avoid incurring an income tax liability of abnormal proportions in good years and defer those liabilities to bad years. The present system of taxation permits some relief to this end but does not go far enough. As well, it gives an inducement to save. At
Grain Stabilization
present, if the individual has a bad year he is allowed to back-average and thus obtain some relief. The problem with this is purely a matter of timing. By the time the individual has received the effect of the carry-back, he may well be through his next year.
We need a plan which would allow an individual to build up a cash reserve, through an individual, registered stabilization fund, which would allow him to have an even flow of cash income and taxable income over the years. The plan would be a self-administered, to be set up within existing government regulations, namely tax legislation, and would not require any red-tape commission to administer it. The government should allow an individual or corporation whose primary business is that of farming to acquire a deposit certificate at any chartered bank, credit union, trust company or treasury branch. The amount of the individual fund deposit should not be greater than 75 per cent of the gross sales of agricultural products, grain, cattle, etc., for the year in question.
The advantages of this type of self-administered program would be these. Producers would save dollars and increase the reserves in our banking system. Producers would spend dollars on a more systematic basis. The program would cause the feast or famine syndrome afflicting farmers to vanish. Finally, the program could be set up at no cost to the taxpayer. Such a program would help to smooth out the economic situation of farmers and the feast or famine situation of the entire Canadian economy, in which I include farm equipment manufacturing, and so on.
The strength of our grain exports is no illusion. These exports are a real and growing force in international relations. They must be used with skill to establish a healthy trading relationship between Canada and the rest of the world. Instead of continually dealing with symptoms, the government should put much more effort into this particular area of endeavour. I have put forward one proposal and the hon. member for Moose Jaw made two others. I hope the government will consider them seriously.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have discussed stabilization a number of times in the House in the last five years, always with the hope that we could develop a system which would stabilize the income of farmers producing a certain commodity and allow them at least to regain their costs of production plus a reasonable return. Canadian farmers have watched with keen interest the machinations of federal and provincial governments with respect to stabilization. Last week the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said that the government had introduced stabilization legislation this year to cover specific commodities. He went on to say:
Stability for the producer will be reflected in stable production and stable prices for consumers. There are many ways, some major and some minor, to bring about this stability. One major advance was the recently passed amendments to the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Effective stabilization legislation encourages rational production decisions. A prairie grain market insurance plan will also help.
His statement is undated, but I think it is safe to assume he made it before the agriculture committee last Tuesday. The bill before us is not a grain marketing insurance plan.

It is complex and is not well understood by most. It will, at best, produce a levelling-off of losses that may flow from the cash flow position of farmers when there is a decrease in certain categories of the grain production industry in western Canada. This bill is difficult to understand. I pointed this out to my colleague who is very interested in the English language. He often refers to the fact that when I first came here I used long sentences.

and divide the product so obtained in respect of such grain by the number of bushels per acre of such grain that is the average yield for such grain for the five years immediately preceding the year under review;
(b)	add the eighteen quotients obtained pursuant to subparagraphs (a) (i), (ii) and (iii); and
(c)	divide the sum obtained pursuant to paragraph (b) by the number of acres on which grain is seeded in the designated area in the year under review.
That is one sentence, Mr. Speaker, I would like the minister to explain it. Possibly Your Honour might like to interpret what it means. In any event, there will be some difficulty. That sentence is not going to help the average farmer in this country to use the average over the five years, and so on. The average farmer is interested in two things. He would like to ascertain how much production he should have, how much acreage he should sow, and wheth-
er he should go with one commodity or another. Second, he wants to know what the market price will be.
For him to be successful in meeting his commitment both to this nation and to the consumers of this nation, he has to produce enough to cover any disaster that may occur from year to year, something that is not covered under the umbrella of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act of which we are disposing. He will have to take into consideration the weather, yield and protein quotient in his production. He must do this knowing that he will be able to pay for the production expenses that he incurs. Secondly, when he reaps his harvest he wants to be assured of a relatively stable market and a price that will pay for his production and provide him and his family with a decent standard of living. That is fairly simple.
We are not asking for very much. Agriculture is a very important part of our production and export market. As stated by other ministers, Canada must be committed to helping those parts of the world which do not have enough production to feed themselves. The Canadian grain market has an immense role to play, and this can only be done when there is stability. Anyone the least bit interested in food production is aware of the need to establish a market price that will pay for the cost of production. Second, we must meet the commitment that we make as a nation to export to those countries not able to produce the required amounts of protein.
Everyone agrees that we must have some stability. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) said that during the recession in 1961 it was western grain production that enabled Canada to get back on the road to recovery. By exporting large quantities of grain we were able to bring in hard cash. Hon. members will recall that many sales were made to countries not normally within our wheat trading bloc, such as Russia, and payments were made in gold. That currency was desperately needed at the time. It played a major role in our recovery in that recession.
There is likely to be little disagreement among farmers and Canadians in general that food production, cereal grains in particular, must play an important and ever-increasing role in Canadian agriculture. In order for that to be possible, we have to ensure that we will be able to sell our products at reasonable prices. It is my feeling that if we were to add the commodities which come under the Wheat Board to those which already come under the Agricultural Stabilization Act, and put the whole thing back under the control of the Minister of Agriculture as it used to be, we would find that the farmers in western Canada would receive a much more reasonable return for their money than they are likely to receive from the legislation before us today.
The reason the government has not acted along these lines is simple. Income stabilization plans have the potential of costing a lot of money, especially if we cannot ensure that production is related to sales prospects. The government might well be placed in a position of having to act as a buying agency at 80 per cent of the average price in the preceding five years. Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this might not be a bad idea. I have for years been interest-

speechtext:
And the originals and the aboriginals, in the theological sense. But it would seem to me that the story of Egypt, where they prepared for ten bad years by collecting the harvest of ten good years, was not more applicable in Egypt than it is today in the modern world of 1975. We have been lucky in Canada, but they have not been so lucky in other parts of the world. There is a surplus in Canada of many cereal commodities and the price is such that many Canadians overeat, particularly in the field of cereals. At the same time, there are others across the world who are badly in need of the protein in our cereal products but who are unable to get it.
I see nothing wrong with the establishment by the Government of Canada of a granary which would provide for the needs both of this country and for our commitments to the rest of the world over a ten-year period. To accomplish this we would have to store grain, though not, as now, at the expense of the farmer. The farmer is already doing this to some extent. If he depended for storage on the Wheat Board and the grain commissioners, we would be disappointed; we would find that there is very little grain stored in the elevators. There is no grain held in the federally-controlled elevators at Moose Jaw and Lethbridge-they are trying to give away those facilities. Most of the grain presently in storage is held either on the farm or in private grain elevators. I presume there is less than a year's supply. Yet we have done nothing as a nation to provide a world food bank to demonstrate in a practical way our wish to help the hungry people of the world.
I suggest that if we were to substitute for the bill before us an agricultural stabilization bill, we would find, in paying 80 per cent of the five-year average, that we might in the foreseeable future be buying stocks of grain and building up a reserve sufficient to establish a barrier against disasters which might occur not only here but in countries abroad.
It seems to me that in any measures taken to stabilize agriculture we must keep in mind the moral commitment made by the Minister of Agriculture at the international food and agriculture organization. We are under a moral obligation to provide the facilities necessary to maintain basic supplies of commodities which we grow in great abundance. No one, it seems to me, disagrees with the idea of stabilizing farm income. If farm income is not stable, it is likely to be difficult to keep people on the farm.
Some hon. members on the other side seem to think the farmers of western Canada are very well off. Some of them think they all have planes and Cadillacs, or both. That really is not true. We have seen many economic disasters in western Canada, and laws have been passed to protect the farmers so that the mortgage holders do not walk off with the actual facilities for agricultural production. We have had our ups and downs. Weather conditions have been severe, and though they have not been so severe in
Grain Stabilization
the past few years in Canada, that is not the case as far as the rest of the world is concerned. So there is no argument that stabilization is necessary.
The bill which is now before us has been presented on a number of other occasions in slightly different forms. It has been called Bill C-74-

speechtext:
One simple proposition would be to refer this measure to the farmers and find out what they think of it. When the committee went to the farmers with this bill there was no support for it in any of the provinces affected. It is true that in some of the provinces there was not much objection, but that was because farmers really did not think it would make much difference one way or the other.
I suggest that the formula being used is so complicated that farmers cannot reasonably be asked to decide whether they are in favour of the bill or not. It is for this reason farmers have been slow in making up their minds whether or not they want to participate in the scheme.
As the minister says, you can check into it or you can check out of it. There are some restrictions, of course, and there have to be otherwise big farmers would take advantage of the scheme by entering when the cost was not high and taking the benefit when the cost was high. It is very doubtful whether there will be widespread and continued support for the legislation. My recommendation is that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), who is piloting the legislation through the House, should be prepared to discuss the matter with the farmers at the Outlook Conference being held in Ottawa next week. He should be prepared to make this a major topic. I have seen the agenda, and it is not on the agenda. If the Federation of Agriculture and representative of other farm organizations who will be attending the conference agree that should certain changes be made they are prepared to support these proposals, then I would not be opposed to the passage of the legislation. The last time the Federation of Agriculture discussed this question they put forward a couple of very important suggestions. These are as follows:
1.	An assessment be made of the position of the sector by the Stabilization Board and discussed in depth with producer representatives for that sector. It should be required that part of this assessment be an examination of production costs in the industry. The development of the necessary statistics and information, and conceptual basis, for such an examination of cost of production should be subject producers.
2.	Following producer consultation, the government be required to issue a statement of its plans and programs for the stabilization of the industry, both for the production period immediately ahead and in an intermediate term context. This announcement should include an assessment of the industry position and outlook, relating this assessment to the stabilization program and plan in terms of the adequacy of that program to ensure stability and a fair level of producer returns. In such a statement stabilization policy per se should be related to other policies and programs, federal and provincial. The stabilization program and plans should contain within it, provisions for necessary adjustments in the target level of returns in the program in response to increases in producer costs and the rates of inflation in the economy, during the production period.
These producer consultations on a commodity basis should be preceded by at least one intensive and comprehensive producer-government

December 12, 1975
Grain Stabilization
examination of the state of the industry, involving provincial governments as well as producers, in which commodity inter-relationships could be examined and the industry situation discussed in relation to an over-all look at trade developments, the general state of the economy and any other relevant considerations.
Stabilization policy should, in short, be handled in such a way that first of all its central focus should be the income adequacy objective. Moreover the planning of stabilization policy should be integrated into an over-all process of improved industry organization and planning (whether such plans be detailed and regulatory, or broad and directional only).
What that says, Mr. Speaker, is that the farmers, the farm organizations, the provincial governments and the federal government should examine stabilization and develop realistic policies to determine how much of any given commodity should be produced, how the costs of the commodity are divided, and the regional difference in cost due to size of production, distance from market and so on, is split. We must then reassess the needs of the industry in terms of production quotas. Then, and only then, can we establish some long-term and short-term directives to deal with the immediate situation as well as the long term.
Anyone who knows anything at all about agriculture will know that during recent months much attention has been focused on the egg marketing legislation. Consumers and consumers' representatives have been making a lot of fuss about producers asking for too much for their eggs. The argument rages between whether his costs are shortterm or he has to lengthen the period of time for which he sets his price, ignoring some of the temporary ups and downs so far as production costs are concerned.
Consumers' representatives have been saying that their costs should be reflected immediately in consumer prices. The producer argues that he is not able to do this on a short-term basis. We have all witnessed the fighting that has gone on between Mrs. Plumptre of the Food Prices Review Board and the Minister of Agriculture. She was questioning the increase of a cent a dozen the same week that the international market for feed grains was dropping. Actually, the price has now dropped and the price of feed grains is fluctuating from day to day, so it may well be that the board will not be able to equalize production costs over the short term.
There are both short-term and long-term objectives to be considered, but it seems to me that in order to eliminate this kind of fluctuation we should first of all keep a healthy, stable agricultural industry in place, we should provide the Canadian public with first-class agricultural commodities at reasonable prices, and we should begin to meet our commitments to those in the international community who are experiencing shortages of both protein and cereals. We have not faced up to our obligation in this regard, and we have not done so for the simple reason that we have not established the capacity to store Canadian grain for future sale.
Once more we have a surplus of powdered milk. At the same time there is a shortage of cheese, butter and fluid milk in Canada. As far as the dairy industry is concerned, the best way it can contribute to the international demand for food is by supplying milk powder, which can be easily transported, distributed without refrigeration and does not need special care. What is more, it does not cost countries less fortunate than we are very much to buy it. This
|Mr. Peters.]
surplus in powdered milk has caused the price of industrial milk to drop.
A few years ago the Minister of Transport introduced a program that paid the farmers to take land out of production. The LIFT program lifted agricultural land out of production because we said that we did not need it. After but one year the price of grain went from $1.75 for No. 1 Northern wheat to $5.95. This suggests to me that the statistics on which the minister has based this legislation are totally inadequate. The government is not setting the right criteria or being of much value in bringing about stability of supply of any given commodity.
We should establish, first of all, how much of our land in this country is suitable for agricultural production. Surely without much difficulty we can stabilize the two standards of land values being used in this country. In Ontario we start with number one land as the best for agricultural production, and as I understand it you could not possibly farm anything less than about number five land in western Canada. It seems they start out backwards to us, or perhaps the other way around. In any event, it seems very simple for the agricultural department to provide one set of standards to be used in Ontario and in all other parts of Canada. In that event, land valued as number five in Saskatchewan would be the same as land valued as number five in Ontario.
My understanding is that something less than one-seventh of the land in Canada is arable, and only about one-fifth is suitable for agricultural production. Perhaps we should have a new land survey in order to determine the exact amount of land in Canada that is suitable for agricultural purposes. The minister of agriculture in the days when ARDA was first brought in, now the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), suggested at the time that we should catalogue or assess the value of land in Canada.

During that discussion I understood we were not talking about the same thing because of different designations. The only point I was making is that the federal government should standardize in respect of land values so that everyone will be talking about the same thing. The situation now confuses the general public as to what kind of land is available. The general public is confused as to the agricultural potential. We, as Canadians, have always said that we can double or triple our agricultural production by doing all sorts of things. I am not sure that we cannot, but I am not sure how far we can go.
Ontario has been referred to as a leader in the field of developing new crops and improving old ones. We in Ontario have been able to develop strains of cereal grains that require a growing season of only 80 days, compared to the old growing season in the range of 105 to 110 days. I understand that some grains require an even shorter growing season. We have done a very good job in developing new strains, which may result in doubling the amount of land suitable for agricultural production. I sometimes think that we in this country have to be convinced that we need a heathy agricultural industry. Once we have been convinced, we should then know how much the land will produce and how much subsidization this production requires. Agriculture in every country in the world is subsidized to some degree.
Our crops take a great deal out of the land and this has to be put back before additional crops can be produced. We only follow that procedure if the price of the crop is sufficient to provide a reasonable return, while covering the cost of fertilizers that put back the minerals and the other necessary things into the land. So far we are only doing this when the price is high. When the price is not high enough to cover the cost of production, these essential ingredients are not returned to the soil. Some lands in Canada are entirely dependent for production on the fertilizers and other things that are put back into them. It is fine for the Minister of Agriculture to travel to the World Food Agency in Rome, making the statement that we will give a certain value in agricultural commodities to the world. We can do this, but only if we know how much we can produce. It seems that we can only do this if prices are such that we can afford to continue putting back into the land what we take out. In this way we can make the maximum use of land available. Once we are able to do that we will be able to meet these commitments.
I disagree with the legislation before us because it contains the phrase "stabilization of income," and starts out by saying it will stabilize net proceeds from the production and sale of western grains, and then refers to certain amendments to statutes as a consequence. Most farmers do not believe this bill will meet net proceeds. This whole thing involves a very complicated production formula which cannot be applied, as this bill intends, to very large areas. Agricultural production in western Canada has historically shown that the net proceeds in one township can vary vastly from the net proceeds in the next township. This has been true in areas where there are such things as

It has been suggested by some persons recently that farmers should go into the production of pigs. I shudder every time I hear an official make a statement that we should move into something that we are not in now when there appears to be a shortage. That was the case in respect of the cow-calf situation. The producers could not obtain enough money from the calf to keep the cow for a year. There now is a suggestion that they should go into the production of pork.
Every housewife knows that the price of bacon and pork is increasing very rapidly. If producers went into the production of pork they would find themselves in a great deal of trouble. If they went into the production of pork today they would be victims of the fluctuations in the grain market, which are quite sizeable and regular. Anyone who went into this on the basis of the price of pork today, I think would find that as the number of pigs increases the market will not be there. The price normally is 50 per cent of the price of beef. I do not think anyone in this country who really looks at the situation would be stupid enough to believe that one could produce pork today at half the price of beef.
All segments are being affected by the stabilization in any one field. I would suggest to the Minister of Transport responsible for this bill that he not stand on his principle, but rather look at the economics of the proposition he is putting forward. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE RATE OF RETURN ON GOVERNMENT ANNUITY CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not take very much time on this matter. As we all know this is a non-controversial bill but I think I should commend the government for bringing in this legislation. The government, of course, should be criticized for the length of time it took in awakening to the problems that have been encountered as a result of the low rate of interest.
I think this bill serves three purposes. It attempts to solve the problem related to the low rate of interest. Second, I think it adds flexibility in that the governor in

council can either lower or raise the rate of return. I understand it does not move in terms of allowing the rate to be lower than that which was originally applicable. The third matter involves the discontinuance of sales because the government, in its wisdom believes that the sales of these annuities has served its purpose. The government believes that the annuities have been superseded by retirement plans in the private sector.
Dealing with the first point I am amazed that the rate of interest encompassed by the legislation is only 7 per cent when we are talking now of an inflationary rate of around 11 per cent. One can see that the purchasing power has been eroded by some 3 per cent or 4 per cent. I am not talking about indexing in this bill, but I am saying that the government should have appreciated the circumstances which exist in terms of hardship when we look at a 7 per cent rate in respect of this bill compared to the inflation rate of 11 per cent.
My second point concerns the discontinuance of sales. The act was first introduced in 1908. The House leader of the New Democratic Party says that the bill was born at the same time he was. I think that is a commendable situation. It shows how long that member has been in and around this House and that since birth he has been interested in pension schemes. He still is. In terms of reviewing his concern in this area may I say that the bill was brought in primarily to give people the idea that thrift is a necessity in our way of life and that they should put something away for their old age. If those principles are still applicable the government should accept that.
Perhaps these sales have to be discontinued because there has not been sufficient promotion and because the rate of return is simply disgraceful. I respectfully submit that the private sector has not in fact taken over the necessary pension schemes that workers should have in Canada. The latest statistics in this area, taken in 1970, indicate that almost 7 per cent of the people employed by private companies are not receiving coverage. Therefore I take a very dim view of the government indicating that we will now get rid of this annuity contract, which in effect is a pension scheme, because the private sector has taken it over in a satisfactory way.
These are the only comments I have. My colleague, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave), will be our only speaker following me with respect to this matter. We appreciate the fact that the government has brought in this bill and we appreciate the thinking behind it, but at the same time we say the government should be chastised for taking so long to realize that such a step was required.
In its recent report the Canadian Council on Social Development criticized the attitude taken by the government in stating, that the private sector has taken over in this respect. It stated that the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec pension plan have been downgraded so that the private sector could carry on, and it has reached the conclusion that there has been a dismal failure in that regard.
The Montreal Gazette of November 27 reported the following in an article:
December 12, 1975

The Canada and Quebec plans should be given the central role in the over-all pension system, it argues. They are popular, straightforward, universal, portable, secure, looked upon as faithful friends by many workers and have the "tremendous advantage" of being indexed upward with the cost of living.

Mr. Speaker, although the answers we received when we were in the standing committee on this bill did not completely satisfy us, the fact is that we did get our questions answered. I think it is appropriate for me to say that we had a very good discussion of this bill at that stage. Accordingly I do not think it is necessary for us to extend the debate at third reading. Indeed we are prepared to give our endorsation to the bill.
I would be less than human if I did not thank the hon. member who has preceded me for referring to the fact that the act itself was debated in the House of Commons on the very day that I was born. So I suppose my interest in matters relating to pensions can be identified as a lifelong interest.
It is true that we would like to have seen improvements of even a better one, particularly with respect to a greater rate of interest, and there are one or two other things that might have been done, but on the whole we think it is a good bill. I may say that the amendments that were made in the committee at the instigation of the government also improved the bill.
My only other comment is in the same area in which comments were made by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), namely, with respect to the old age security picture as a whole. I think it is timely that the Canadian Council on Social Development produced its voluminous report a short while ago on the state of retirement pensions in this country, and I think it is particularly relevant that in that report emphasis is placed on the need to extend the role of the Canada Pension Plan in the retirement security of our people.
I had to say in the committee that I did not agree with the statement made in the name of the minister that private pension plans have taken over the role of extra security for our people. The fact that so few contracts under the government annuity system are now being purchased is due, I think, more to the fact that we have the Old Age Security Act, and the Canada Pension Plan now, which of course had not even been thought of when this legislation was introduced back in 1908.
But the report to which both the previous speaker and I have referred is, in my view, dead on when it urges a review of our whole retirement policy, and particularly in its urging that the Canada Pension Plan be enlarged so that adequate security will really be available to all our people, not just to those who can purchase supplemental benefits, whether from government or private sources. This is a measure of the progress that we made in these 67 years. All that parliament could do 67 years ago was to provide, under government auspices, a means whereby those who could afford it could do something about their old age. We have moved from that to the point where we realize that it is our social responsibility to see that something is done under the aegis of the government for the adequate retirement and adequate security of all our older people.
Government Annuities
One thing I do not like happening is to see something taken away before something else has been put in its place. The something else that should be in place of this plan is a greatly enlarged Canada Pension Plan which provides much more than the 25 per cent pension that it now provides.
I hope that this action, together with a study of the volume produced by the Canadian Council on Social Development, will lead to early legislation along the lines suggested in that document. For the moment, however, we are prepared to give our support to the passing of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a very brief comment on the government annuity bill, C-75, at its third reading. As the two members who have preceded me indicated, I feel it is a very worthwhile bill. My particular interest stems from the fact that I happen to be one of those contract holders, and have been for quite a number of years, although not nearly as far back as the first speaker, and I have a personal interest which provokes these remarks.
I am particularly concerned with the retroactive date of April, 1975, and I would like to suggest that the government has in fact admitted the inadequacy of its annuity policy by the very fact of bringing in this bill to which we are now giving third reading. I am critical only of the retroactive date, and I suggest that surely it could have been at least one year earlier, and I say this very sincerely. I raised this point in committee, and the chairman of the committee in response to my question stated that the only reason they did not make it go back to an earlier date was the cost, which would amount to $38 million for the year.
I suggest that when these contracts were taken out in the earlier days-in my case it was around 1940-they were considered a very good, solid, long-term investment. There was no high powered sales job done at that time to encourage people to buy government investments. They were considered a really good investment. Over the last few years I have received, as I am sure other members have, many complaints from constituents about the low rate of return on these contracts. I can appreciate the need to phase out this policy, but I think the government might have been a little more considerate of the people who bought a contract and supported the government in their own way, and who now have such a low rate of return.
I wanted to put those views on the record, but in spite of that I certainly support this type of legislation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL ACT AND TO AUTHORIZE CONTINUATION OF PENSIONS PAID BY COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may seem strange to most hon. members that before this parliament winds up its normal course in a couple of years time, the great explosion which shook the city of Halifax will at that time have been 60 years in our past. At that time, with the present rate mortality among those receiving help under the Halifax Relief Commission, it is likely that there will still be some four dozen people benefiting from the activities of the commission.
I do not propose to detain the House long with my contribution. It represents the distillation of consultation between the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who is the hon. member for Halifax, and myself, on the few points we would like to make, and I think these are points which can usefully be answered in committee.
Four of these points actually come to my mind. The first is that under the new set up one should be alert to ensure that the pensions provide are adequate. Our understanding is that they are really based on the same circumstances as if these people had been injured in the front lines of the first world war, but whatever the formula it should certainly provide quick and adequate remedies for those who receive the pensions.
The second point is that upon this change being made there should be a review of the scale of pensions being offered.
The third point is that the machinery, which is going from a set-up where pensioners can march down the street, as it were, and deal with people they have known for a long period of time, and which no doubt will be replaced by something else, should be equally as humane and equally as accessible.
The fourth point is really an extension of the third, and that is that the minister should set up some special tele-

phone number or location to which the pensioners could write with their problems. I say this because the Canadian Pension Commission is probably too large a concept for these pensioners to deal with if they are trying to chase someone in the Halifax telephone book in that large section which deals with the Government of Canada. In other words, there should be some instantly accessible source to which these people can turn with their requests for the help the Halifax Relief Commission has afforded to them over the years.
Finally, when dealing with this issue it is always customary for public figures to ask what happens if there is any money left over when all the claims have been met and the last claimant has passed on. I note that the bill provides that if anything should be left over, it should go toward municipal works or municipal action in that part of Halifax which was devastated by the explosion. I have no quarrel with that concept, but I think there are too many people in Canada who have lost sight of the fact that if it had not been for the very generous contributions which came from Boston, Massachusetts, and other parts of New England, but particularly Boston-what we in the Mari-times call the Boston states-the Halifax Relief Commission would not have prospered so well over the years. The generosity of Americans to the city of Halifax in its greatest hour of need is something I personally will never forget, and I hope others will never forget either.
