speechtext:
I thank my hon. friends who are trying to get attention to what I am saying.
Before I get to my specific question I wish to emphasize, as the previous speaker has done, that although the Halifax explosion of December 6, 1917, took place a long time ago, there are still 50 or 60 persons who are drawing pensions or assistance of one kind or another. I believe the total number of persons killed in the explosion was in the
December 12, 1975

order of 1,800 and during the years some 1,250 persons have been on pensions of one kind or another.
The problem which still obtains for survivors I think is well set out in a letter which I have before me, from a correspondent of mine who was four years old when the explosion took place. That would make him about one year older than the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). Although I was nine years old at the time, I remember hearing about the explosion, even away out on the west coast where we were living. I have this letter from this man who is now 62 years old and has been blind for the 58 years since the explosion took place. He says in part:
In discussing the events of the Halifax explosion most people find it incredible that so much suffering did occur in many of the north end Halifax families. In my immediate family my grandfather and his oldest son were killed, my grandmother lost her sight, one daughter lost her hearing plus the sight of one eye, another daughter lost a foot and the youngest son lost his sight. In my family I lost my sight and forty-six of my father's relatives, brothers, sisters, aunts and uncles, were killed.
Later in the letter he says:
Most people regard the Halifax explosion as ancient history but to me it is still very real.
The difficulty of this correspondent is that although he has been paid a pension from that fund for many years, the pension has not been increased to keep pace with the rising cost of living or the rising standard of living. It is his concern today that he should be granted a pension similar to what would have been granted, as the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants suggested, if he had been a person hurt in the front line of war. That has been the theory and rationale behind the fund, but many survivors feel that it has not been carried out. I hope that the transfer of these funds and responsibilities from the Halifax Relief Commission to the Canadian Pension Commission will not result in the books being closed.
That brings me to some particular questions I should like to hear answered in specific terms. Bill C-78 provides for the money in the fund to be turned over to the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), and for the administration of the fund to be undertaken by the Canadian Pension Commission, which also deals with the disability pensions of those who served in war. The language of the preamble includes the following words:
. .. and the Canadian Pension Commission to continue the payment of pensions, grants or allowances to those who suffered as a result of the explosion;...
Clause 3(2) of the bill empowers the Canadian Pension Commission to:
pay a pension, a grant or an allowance to any person who the Canadian Pension Commission determines is eligible to receive a pension, a grant or an allowance in respect of death or injury sustained in the explosion at Halifax in 1917.
What I wish to know is this: does that authority merely mean that the Canadian Pension Commission can continue to pay what has already been authorized, or will the commission be given these two other elements of authority? Will it be able to escalate pensions now being received and increase those payments where they have fallen far behind the rise in the cost of living? Second, will the Canadian
Halifax Relief Commission
Pension Commission have authority to pay a new pension or new pensions? Even after all these years, one or more of the survivors might demonstrate that there should be such a provision.
In addition, we must consider what happens to the survivors of the survivors. In the meantime, these people have married, raised families, and so on. Are they to be regarded as though they were in the front line at the time of the Halifax explosion in 1917? Will they be given that sort of treatment?
The idea of winding up the commission seems sensible. I notice that there is provision for the pensions of those who have worked on this commission. Also the idea of turning the administration over to the Canadian Pension Commission makes sense. Actually, I have received representations asking this to be done. But I want to know if the Canadian Pension Commission will simply be a bookkeeping office that carries on what has already been set out, or will it be authorized to make increases, or even, if this is called for, to provide for new pension payments.
The other point I make in passing is one to which the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants referred. What will be done with the money when the need for it ends? It seems reasonable to propose that it should then be turned back to an appropriate authority in Halifax, for the continued rehabilitation of the area of the city damaged in the 1917 Halifax explosion. As I say, I was a boy of nine at the time. I mention this, so that hon. members will not think that I am older than I really am. My family had come from Nova Scotia, but we were away on the west coast when this tragedy took place, and we were concerned.
I think it is appropriate that, many years later, we should spend this afternoon in the House of Commons recalling the suffering of those affected by the explosion and recalling, as the previous speaker did, the contributions which came in from all over Canada, New England and the United Kingdom, to help the people of Halifax in their time of need.
We support this bill gladly; if I could get an assurance that my questions will be answered I would not mind if the House went into committee of the whole to deal with the bill. But if we must send the bill to a standing committee, to get answers to questions the previous speaker and I have raised, then of course, we shall agree to that being done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a few comments to the House at this time on third reading of this bill to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. I wish to say at the outset that I do so on behalf of the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), who is unable to be here today. I mention that because of the very excellent background work the hon. member performed which helped all members of the Standing Committee on Agriculture when they were considering this bill. Because of his background as a veterinarian I think it is appropriate that I mention the work which he did on this particular bill.
We on this side, as I am sure do most members of the House, support the bill. The only critical comment I can make is that it took the government so long to bring it to this final stage. First reading took place on October 21, 1974, well over a year ago. It is perhaps appropriate to note that this is fairly typical of the low priority given to new agricultural legislation. Perhaps we fail to appreciate the

genuine importance and value of agriculture in Canada today.
The members of the standing committee certainly appreciated the work done by, and the co-operation received from the various branches of the Department of Agriculture. I mention in particular the Health of Animals Branch. This bill amends an act which is over 100 years old. By the very nature of the Contagious Diseases Act, the Health of Animals Branch must be very closely involved.
I speak with some knowledge of various cattlemen's associations across Canada. They too had the co-operation of the Health of Animals Branch with regard to the many representations they made to the department on this bill. I am sure the same applies to other branches of the Department of Agriculture.
I wish to refer to the concern of cattlemen with regard to the shipment of calves from western Canada to Ontario and points east of Montreal. After many years, this legislation will now make it legal to ship calves a little faster from western Canada by way of Winnipeg and Toronto to their final destinations, mostly in Ontario. For many years there has been an obstruction in getting calves shipped here quicker and, consequently, getting them here in a healthier condition.
At one time trainloads of cattle had to be stopped every 36 hours for a feed and rest period. Through mutual understanding, and I stress that as it involves the co-operation of the humane societies, it is now recognized that if calves can travel faster and without unnecessary stops, they can go for periods of 42 to 58 hours, and perhaps longer. The theory is that the quicker they get to their final destination, even when longer hauls are required, the better the health of the cattle will be. This legislation makes this possible. It takes the authority for those regulations out of the Department of Justice and gives it to the Department of Agriculture where it belongs.
This bill will update considerably the amount of compensation for animals that fall down on the brucellosis test. This is a very timely topic. We have heard a lot in this House and across the country about brucellosis over the past two or three years, particularly the past six months. Questions asked in the House clearly indicate there have been some problems with brucellosis.
It was reassuring to hear from the representatives of the Health of Animals Branch who appeared before the committee that progress is indeed being made. I believe more progress will be made, and possibly there will be a complete eradication of brucellosis. As this bill provides higher compensation to cattle producers, hopefully there will be better co-operation. After all, when the compensation is not very high there is a tendency not to advise the proper authorities that there may be brucellosis in the herd. Therefore this is a very forward step.
I hope this spirit of co-operation between the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the various branches of his department will continue when the regulations are being drawn up. They will of course be very detailed and involved. I am sure that many agricultural commodity groups will want the opportunity to take part in a continuing discussion when the regulations are being drawn up.
December 12, 1975

With those few comments, Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise that we in the official opposition clearly support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that there is not much time to discuss the bill before us because I think it is a very important one.
Canadians should be very proud of what we have been able to do in the one hundred years this legislation has been in existence in terms of eradicating animal diseases from the Canadian scene. I suppose it is possible to say that if Dr. Ken Wells, Veterinary Surgeon-General, had been in charge of medicine in this country over the last number of years we would have eradicated many diseases rather than having just found methods of treating them. I presume some of our major diseases would by now have come under test procedures which would enable us to discover and eliminate diseases early. I do not know whether he would have been able to arrive at suitable compensation if his work involved human beings in the same way he has been able to do it with animals. But he certainly has been successful, Mr. Speaker, and maybe we should be looking at that method of getting rid of some of the-

Mr. Speaker, much of this bill is involved with compensation, and I suppose that if we were looking at eradication in any field that would be a factor. But I approve the suggestions which have been made and the major decision which has been made with regard to brucellosis, bearing in mind that vaccination has the unfortunate side effect of creating carriers and the knowledge that under vaccination the eradication of brucellosis will not be entirely possible. Eradication will hopefully allow us to establish completely free zones in Canada which will enable us to continue the same degree of export as has been possible over the years simply because of our control of the disease. We have controlled brucellosis, tuberculosis, and many other diseases in this way and I am pleased to see the department has now taken a look at some of the other factors which have developed involving the health of animals.
One of the major problems affecting animals has been that of safe and humane transportation. Stories have appeared in the newspapers over the last few years of cattle arriving at destinations in a very unsatisfactory condition; quite often a number had died. This matter, I believe, is to be looked after by suitable controls which are to be established.
Two other segments have been added which will put the Veterinary Surgeon-General in a position of looking after
Business of the House
the health of human beings as well. You know, with the very poor rates of benefit being paid to some senior citizens some have felt the need to conserve their money to the extent that they have been eating food designated for animal pets, and there have been abuses of the regulations which have been in force over the years in that field. Now new regulations will be made to control that situation, not only for pets but for others who may find it more advantageous to buy pet food for human consumption than to do without entirely. The controls we are putting into the animal food compartment raise many problems that are related to this bill, but the initiative being shown by the veterinary staff in their willingness to supervise animal plant food, is to be commended.
The controls which have been extended to the rendering plants also is in the same field, since it affects human beings. There have been cases where food designated for pet food factories and rendering plants has been made into other products such as fertilizer, meal, etc. Those are now being controlled by the department and it seems to me this may eliminate, in provinces where there is no provincial control, the danger of some of the meat finding its way into human consumption. The Veterinary Surgeon-General may find himself the largest supervisor in the Olympics when he looks after the hamburger and hot dog fields. Any control which assures to Canadians that meat designated for disposal otherwise than for human consumption stays exactly in that field, which has not been the case in the past few years, is most welcome.
I concede therefore by repeating that this is a very worth-while bill'. I would like to congratulate the veterinary service on the work they have done in controlling animal diseases in Canada. We have an enviable reputation, and extending their supervision into those fields where abuses have taken place in the past is worthy of support, and we certainly like to give praise where it is due.
The veterinary staff has been very competent in doing a good job on behalf of Canadians and by giving them this bill, and the increases that are made in compensation, we may ensure that progress wherever possible can be made in the control of contagious diseases. This is a field into which they themselves did not want to get, but no other national agency is controlling the rendering and pet food industry. Control will certainly be welcome there also.

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Kenora-Rainy River) moved
subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
that Bill S-30, to incorporate the Continental Bank of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to thank the House for allowing me to proceed with this bill this afternoon; it is a courtesy I appreciate very much.
The bill before us is a complicated one, one that I believe the House and its committee will want to look at very closely. In fact as sponsor of the bill I would advise members of that committee to examine it under a very powerful microscope. The reason is that the bill takes an already existing financial institution incorporated under the various provincial laws and incorporates it into a bank, a somewhat different institution.
To my knowledge this is the first time that a retail sales finance company has attempted to convert itself into a bank. Indeed, to my knowledge, it is the first time that any other financial institution has attempted to convert itself into a bank. Consequently, because we are taking an existing business and converting it into something else, the bill provides for a series of transitional periods and alters a number of very important aspects of the Bank Act in order to transform an existing business into something else.
I do not want to describe to the House all of the exceptions that are contained in the bill, but I do want to give some brief history of the company and to indicate what are some of the changes proposed in the bill in order to convert the IAC into a chartered bank.
First of all I think it important to indicate that IAC is a Canadian institution. At one time, when it first originated, it was an American institution, but 50 years ago the American owners pulled out and a group of Canadians took it over. Under their leadership the company has prospered. At the present time some 12,000 Canadians own 96 per cent of the common shares of the company, amounting to approximately 13.5 million shares.
The business of the company is extensive. Some 65 percent is in business financing, 16 per cent in sales financing, 10 per cent in consumer loans, and 9 per cent in residential mortgages. I think it important to recognize that a substantial portion of IAC's present business is in areas covered
Continental Bank
by chartered banks at the present time. In point of fact 70 per cent of the assets of IAC result from activities which are normally considered to be the preserve of the chartered banks in Canada.
It is also important to realize that IAC is a financial institution of substantial size. According to the figures I have here IAC with assets of $2,139.5 million ranks 11th in size among Canadian financial institutions, with an equity base of $203.6 million. When one is looking at institutions that are larger one finds names such as the Royal Bank of Canada, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, the Bank of Montreal, the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Toronto-Dominion Bank.Banque Canadienne Nationale, the Royal Trust Company, Banque Provinciale du Canada, the Huron and Erie Mortgage Corporation, and the Canada Permanent Mortgage Corporation, then followed by IAC, with the 12th on the list being General Motors Acceptance Corporation of Canada, Limited, which has its indebtedness guaranteed by U.S. parent corporations.
When we are dealing with IAC we are dealing with an organization that is indeed of some considerable size. It is quite clear that if the bank does obtain its charter it will have a substantial chance of being able to provide services across the country. IAC carries on business now at 270 locations in all ten provinces and the Yukon. It employs 2,800 people at those locations, and has four divisional headquarters at Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver.
There are a number of changes or exceptions to the Bank Act which are being proposed under this bill. I think it only fair to indicate to the House what some of those exceptions are; exceptions which I am sure the House will want to examine. For example, Section 7(3) allows a period of two years for full compliance with Section 18 of the Bank Act prescribing qualifications of directors. The Bank Act prohibits directors of banks, deposit-taking institutions and similar financial organizations from being directors of another bank. Ten out of the 19 directors of IAC fall into this category. For sound practical and financial reasons, IAC has requested this two-year period to permit the orderly phasing out of these ten directors. This is a question I think the committee will want to investigate quite carefully.
Another section the committee may want to look at is Section 15(4), which permits a four-year period within which shareholders holding more than the 10 per cent maximum permitted by the Bank Act would be allowed to continue to hold and vote their shares. At the present time there is only one shareholder who fits into this category, but again this is something that members may want to look at; that is, a means of easing the financial difficulties of transferring substantial numbers of shares from one shareholder to others.
There are also other questions I think the committee will want to look at, particularly Section 18(11) which deals with the relationship between the Continental Bank and IAC Limited during the transitional period. Both institutions would be in existence during this transitional period while Continental is being built up by the infusion of assets from IAC, and IAC in turn is being run down.

Continental Bank
I do not want to take more time going into the details of the bill except to indicate to hon. members in all fairness that it is most complex, dealing with a very complex subject. The details of the bill have been worked out by the company and by officials of the government, particularly those responsible for administering the Bank Act and for supervising the activities of banks.
I want to say one of the things that interests me about this project is the fact that it is complicated and that it will provide an opportunity for the House of Commons to look at the difficulties and the potential of banking financial institutions in Canada moving from one agency into another. This will allow the House of Commons to deal with this question of setting its own guidelines on the form it would like to see for such conversions in the future, if indeed the House makes that decision. I hope the committee will be able to give careful consideration to this proposal. It is a worth-while proposal, one which I commend to the House and the committee. I hope it will result in the development by the House of a policy to deal with situations like this in future.

speechtext: The hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville (Mr. Nystrom).

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: You sure did well yesterday in Vancouver. Tell us about British Columbia, Lome.

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to hear the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) get up and tell us all about his new Social Credit membership card and his new party alliance. I would remind him that the Social Credit party will be holding a national leadership convention very soon and I am sure he would make an acceptable candidate for that job. In fact he would go over very well. He would fit right into the mainstream of that new, grand alliance in the province of British Columbia.
I would like to say a word or two about the bill before us today.

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Get back to the heady, high financial aspects.

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
The idea occurred to me last night when I heard the results coming in about the new alliance in British Columbia that perhaps the day had come when the Liberal and Conservative parties in the House should move to make the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) the Prime Minister, formalizing the alliance federally as well as in the province of British Columbia.
The bill before us today is one that once again deals with banking. Let me comment at the outset that there are a lot of questions to be answered here that none of us can answer. As the parliamentary secretary has said, this is a new endeavour which is going in a new direction. This step will make the Industrial Acceptance Corporation, with assets of $2.1 billion, as referred to by the parliamentary secretary, the new Continental Bank.
I do not see the need for any more privately owned banks in this country, and I hesitate to change the rules of banking until we have had a chance to study the changes during the decennial review of the Bank Act in 1977. For reasons of that kind I do not really think we should be in a

hurry to get this bill through the House. I realize this bill is going to raise a lot of questions and, therefore, I have no opposition to referring it to the standing committee. I look forward to discussing the bill in the committee with the parliamentary secretary and other members. Hopefully we can learn a lot from that study and make some decisions that will help us in reviewing the Bank Act in 1977.
As I said yesterday, or the day before in the House, I would like to take a whole new look at financial institutions in terms of making them publicly owned institutions. To me the banks and financial institutions have a tremendous say in what happens in this country. They have an awful lot of economic clout. They work in many cases hand in hand with multi-national corporations, and they have objectives and priorities that are based along the same lines as those of large corporations. They are profit and corporate motivated, and I think that is wrong.
I would like to see a big bank in this country owned by all the people of Canada, operated as a public utility or a publicly owned institution. That is the direction I think we should be going. Therefore I do not feel any need to co-operate in the formation of a new bank.
I do not want at this time to hold up the bill. I should like to see it get to the committee in order that we might have a chance to ask a lot of questions, and a chance to offer some amendments. In this way we might have a real chance to find out the purpose of the Industrial Acceptance Corporation in wanting to make this move. There are a lot of questions to which I want answers. I want to know who the primary stockholders are; who owns the corporation, and who sits on the board of directors. I want to know what positions they hold with other banks and other financial institutions. In addition, I want to know who they have in the Senate; are there any senators who sit on the board of directors of this company?
Once again I note that this is a bill which originates in the other place. I have said in the House before, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said on many occasions, I do not see the need for the existence of the other place, and to me it is a slight to see a bill originating in or introduced by the other place. That is not a democratic institution, but one that we think should not exist. It is a place I think has many conflicts of interest, particularly when it comes to a financial bill or a bank bill. Many of those people sitting in the other place are sitting or have sat on the boards of directors of many financial institutions or banks, dealing with bills concerning banking. To me that is a gross conflict of interest. I think this House should deal with all bills that come before us in a public sense, particularly those that deal with banks and financial institutions.
As I say, I do not want to hold the bill up. I am looking forward to dealing with it in the committee, if it goes to the committee, as I look forward to dealing with similar bills involving banking and financial institutions that come before this House in the years ahead.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say that it seems to be the view of the House that this bill should be sent to the committee.
December 12, 1975

I agree there are certain clauses of the bill which require careful scrutiny by the Committee. I also agree there should not be provisions in the bill if, as, and when it finally passes which I expect it will, which amount to exceptions to the Bank Act other than exceptions of a transitional nature demanded by the particular situation. I would agree that changes of a permanent nature in respect of the Bank Act should be made in the course of a review of that act.
Generally I favour incorporation of an additional bank. I would have to disagree with my hon. friend in the New Democratic Party who just spoke. I think the more competition there is in the banking business of this country the better. I think there should be more sources of financial credit available to Canadian individuals and Canadian businesses, large and small. The hon. member also indicated a desire that Canadian banks be publicly owned. I do not want to provoke an argument at this stage on Friday afternoon but I suggest to him that times have passed him by, that he has been by-passed by developments in advanced theory.
I think it is now pretty well agreed in most countries that ownership does not give control. I do not wish to push the argument too far, but I would ask the hon. gentleman to reflect on how much control there is by Canadians over the Bank of Canada or the Canadian National Railways. I understand, for example, that in Great Britain the government has been able to exercise virtually any degree of control it wishes over private enterprise but finds itself almost completely helpless in controlling or operating the enterprises it owns. I suggest it is high time there was a little re-thinking done about how the public maintains most effective control where it is necessary, and perhaps a little examination of whether it is not considerably a myth to think that ownership by a government as such really provides the people with any meaningful degree of control over large companies. However, I do not rise to provoke an argument. I am just trying to do my little bit in educating a younger member of the House.

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: The hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise).

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Another younger member.

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I was not informed long enough in advance that we would be considering this bill today; it was determined only this afternoon. I do not intend for my part to object to this bill being referred to committee for consideration. This bill I am sure deserves lengthy consideration. The Social Credit Party of Canada is reluctant with respect to the Canadian monetary system. That does not mean that we have something against banks or bank owners but we do have something against the legislation which allows banks to create and control credit in Canada. The leader of the opposition said earlier that having more chartered banks would allow a better control to be exercised. I wondered somewhat if he would not go as far as suggesting that we each have our own bank or piggybank. There would be a good opposition,
Continental Bank
and we could all have our own credit. I do not think it goes that far; I do not know exactly who are the shareholders. I do not know them myself but I think IAC is well known in Canada. It is precisely that company which wants to be incorporated as a bank to get a charter in Canada.
Well, Mr. Speaker, usually when a company or a group of men ask for a bank charter the appropriate bill is rather limited. Bill S-30 is indeed rather voluminous probably because it has to do with a company which already exists and wants a charter transfer. That is why we will have a lot of questions to ask the representatives of IAC when they appear before the committee of the House and we will certainly take that opportunity to voice our opinions on the way currency and credit should be created and controlled in Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have just one short bit to add to this very interesting discussion. When the bill goes to the committee there should be a method whereby the promoters of this bank will be required to live up to their undertakings. I am sorry to say this has not been the case in respect of the most recent bank which came before this House. The promoters in that case gave undertakings which they have not lived up to. I think this is a contempt not only of parliament but also of the Inspector of Banks and so on. I hope when the bill gets to the committee the undertakings will be given and that the Inspector of Banks will be given the responsibility to see that the undertakings are lived up to after the seal of approval is given, if it is, by parliament. Otherwise a mockery will be made of our system. I for one regret that these undertakings were not fulfilled in the last instance.

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall speak for just a moment. Generally I agree that the addition of further banking opportunities in this country is important in order to accelerate the degree of economic activity in the private sector. I share both the concern of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and the development or the experience as pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield).

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext: You cannot sit on both sides.

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am not attempting to. I think it is exceedingly difficult to control these institutions in the traditional way in which an attempt has been made to control them through public ownership. I think a vital question we will have to face at the next revision of the Bank Act will be the degree of influence available concerning the transactions and general activity of the banks in this country. As was mentioned a moment ago, there is a concern about the degree to which investments are made in this country and whether there are pressures which exist from outside the country.
One final point I believe is vital in terms of the banking institutions of Canada. I refer to the degree to which these institutions adequately reflect the financial needs of the various parts of the country. I think we will have to look very carefully at the way in which the financial portfolios are dealt with by the major banks inasmuch as we still

have the problem of making sufficient capital available in some of the underdeveloped regions of the country. If the banks have not yet found sufficient means of their own to achieve this, then I think some assistance and direction will have to be given. This is something that I hope will be kept in mind in the creation of the new Continental Bank of Canada.
I hope there is not some kind of irony in that the initials of this new bank will be the CBC, inasmuch as we are already spending a good deal of public funds through that particular agency. We want to be sure that the way in which this bank is operating will achieve some measure of economic stimulation and activity.
As a final point let me say that this week there has been a national meeting of two boards of directors of two national banks in this country with respect to their investment portfolios abroad. Very serious questions are being raised about the investment that takes place on the part of these banks in countries with which we have serious disagreements, such as South Africa. I think we do not want to encourage banks that will be investing the individual resources of the depositors of this country in areas where a measure of basic inequality has been maintained, based on something as unacceptable to the people of this country as racial division and separation.
With those few remarks, I look forward to further study of this proposal when it comes before the committee.
